metaDescription: Six nitrile coated gardening gloves compared on liner gauge, foam coating, pack size and wrist design for planting, weeding and light yard chores.
introParagraphs: Nitrile is the quiet workhorse of garden gloves. It is a synthetic rubber that resists oils, wears better than latex, and does not trigger latex allergies, so when a garden store hangs a rack of dipped gloves, most of them are nitrile over a knit liner. What you pay for beyond the coating is mostly the liner: how thin it is, how it stretches, how many pairs come in the pack and how the wrist is finished.

The six pairs here share that nitrile palm but differ in character. The Showa Atlas 370 is the classic four-pack with a coloured nylon liner and an ultra-light feel. The PROMEDIX is a four-pair pack with thickened fingertips and extended cuffs. The WHEATHUSK is a 100-pair bulk pack for groups, the LOCCEF is a micro-foam nitrile glove with a seamless liner, the Wells Lamont is a five-pack on a 13 gauge polyester shell and the NEOTRIL is a three-pair microfoam pack on a seamless nylon shell.

We evaluated each pair from its listing specifications and buyer feedback themes, so every material, gauge and pack size is as the maker describes it. Nitrile on a thin knit is built for dexterity and grip, not for thorns or heavy impact, so we point out where each pair stops being the right glove.

products.name: Showa Atlas 370 Garden Club Nitrile Gloves, 4 Pack
products.description:
The Showa Atlas 370 is a long-running garden glove and the one most gardeners recognize. The listing describes a palm nitrile coating over four different coloured nylon liners, a feel the maker calls optimal dexterity, and an ultra-light, elastic, low-lint glove that resists deformation. The size reviewed here is medium, and the colors vary by pack.

The liner is the reason people keep buying them. A nylon liner is thin, stretches with the hand and keeps its shape through wash after wash, and a low-lint finish means fewer fibers on your hands and in your seed trays. The palm coating covers the part that touches soil and tools and leaves the back of the hand open to air. In a pack of four colors, one pair per family member or per task becomes easy.

The glove is for light work. Nitrile on a thin shell will not stand up to rose thorns, and a sharp twig can pierce it. Compared with the LOCCEF, the Atlas leans on the lighter weight and color-coded pack, and next to the PROMEDIX it has no stated extended cuff. Hand wash it, air dry it and keep it out of strong sun.
products.bestFor: Everyday planting, potting and weeding where a light, dexterous glove is wanted.
pros: Ultra-light nylon liner with good stretch
Palm coating grips tools and pots
cons: Thin shell offers no thorn defense

products.name: PROMEDIX P 4 Pairs Foamed Nitrile Coated Gardening Gloves
products.description:
The PROMEDIX adds two thoughtful details to a standard nitrile glove. The listing describes a lightweight, breathable knit made from premium nylon, a soft yet sturdy foamed nitrile coating, thickened fingertips and extended flexible cuffs that offer protection against thorns, scratches, grime and debris. It comes as a four-pair pack for men and women.

Fingertips are where gloves fail first, since they take the abuse of pinching, scratching and pulling. Thickening that area extends the life of the whole glove. Extended cuffs are a similar practical idea: they cover a bit of the wrist, where soil and twigs creep in while you reach under a shrub. Foamed nitrile gives a grippier surface than a smooth dip.

The maker's thorn language is a listing statement and a thin foamed coating over a knit will not stop a hooked rose thorn. Compared with the Atlas, the PROMEDIX has reinforced tips and a longer cuff but no color coding, and compared with the Wells Lamont it uses nylon rather than polyester. Wash it gently and let it dry flat.
products.bestFor: Weeding and general chores where fingertip wear and wrist debris are the usual problems.
pros: Extended flexible cuffs cover the wrist
cons: Thin coating does not stop heavy thorns
No gauge stated in the listing

products.name: LOCCEF MicroFoam Nitrile Coated Safety Work Gloves, 6 Pairs
products.description:
The LOCCEF is a work glove adopted by gardeners because of its thin, grippy build. The listing describes a micro-foam nitrile coating compatible with light oils that gives a good grip and abrasion resistance, an ultrathin breathable design with water repellent performance, a seamless liner and a knit wrist that stops dirt and debris. The version here is a six-pair pack in size 9 large.

Micro-foam is finer than ordinary foam, which makes the surface feel smoother while still gripping. A seamless liner removes the stitching that can rub the fingers raw during repetitive work, a real comfort plus for long sessions of weeding or transplanting. Six pairs is a generous quantity that suits workshops, community plots or households that use gloves for more than the garden.

It is a safety work glove at heart, so garden-specific features such as cuffs or decorative designs are absent, and sizing is listed as a number. Compared with the Atlas, the LOCCEF is a plainer work glove with more pairs, and next to the NEOTRIL it is a similar micro-foam build. Wash it by hand and replace pairs as the coating wears thin.
products.bestFor: Long sessions of repetitive planting and sorting where a seamless thin glove reduces rubbing.
pros: Micro-foam nitrile grips oily and damp items
cons: Size is listed by number only

products.name: Wells Lamont Men's Nitrile Coated High Dexterity Work Gloves, 5 Pack
products.description:
The Wells Lamont five-pack is the traditional work-glove approach in nitrile. The listing describes a tough nitrile coated palm that resists abrasion, cuts and snags, a flexible knit wrist that keeps dirt and debris out, and a lightweight, breathable 13 gauge polyester knit shell that the maker calls comfortable for long hours. It is sold in large for men.

Thirteen gauge is a fine knit, which means the glove has more stitches per inch and feels thinner against the skin. That is a big help for finishing tasks like tying plants or handling small hardware, and it also means the nitrile sits on a smoother surface. Five pairs in a pack is a sensible number for a household that does yard work, painting and light repairs.

It is a work glove, so the sizing and style lean toward men, and there are no garden-specific extras. Compared with the PROMEDIX, the Wells Lamont has a recognized brand and polyester shell but no stated fingertip reinforcement. Compared with the WHEATHUSK, it is a more considered build in a smaller pack. Machine wash according to the label and air dry.
products.bestFor: Men's general yard and household work where a fine-gauge nitrile glove is wanted in volume.
pros: 13 gauge shell is thin and flexible
Nitrile palm resists abrasion and snags
cons: Men's sizing may be large for some

products.name: NEOTRIL MicroFoam Nitrile Coated Safety Work Gloves, 3 Pairs
products.description:
The NEOTRIL is a compact trio of microfoam nitrile gloves with a seamless shell. The listing says the microfoam nitrile coating on the palm and fingers provides reliable grip and control in damp, wet and oily conditions, the 13 gauge seamless knit nylon shell and microfoam coating offer comfort and a 360 degree range of motion, and the gloves are machine washable and quick drying for light duty tasks.

Machine washability is the practical highlight. Gardening gloves collect mud, plant sap and sweat, and a glove that can go in the wash with a regular load is far more likely to be kept clean. The seamless shell cuts down the rubbing that makes thin gloves irritating, and the nylon dries quickly after a rinse. The microfoam coating helps with wet stems and slippery pots.

Three pairs is a small pack by the standards of this group, and the glove is clearly marketed for light duty work. Next to the LOCCEF, the NEOTRIL is a similar build with fewer pairs but a stated wash instruction, and next to the Atlas it is less colourful but more utilitarian. Replace pairs when the coating peels at the thumb.
products.bestFor: Easy-care everyday gardening where machine washing and quick drying are priorities.
pros: 360 degree range of motion per the listing
cons: Only three pairs in the pack

products.name: WHEATHUSK 100 Pack Breathable Nitrile Rubber Coated Gardening Gloves
products.description:
The WHEATHUSK is a bulk pack of one hundred pairs, a different animal from the rest of the lineup. The listing describes nitrile rubber coated gloves roughly 23 centimeters long, with a nitrile coating for a non-slip grip on dry or wet tools and materials, and a wrinkled coating surface that improves anti-slip performance and provides resistance to oil and water.

A hundred pairs is a plan, not a purchase. It suits community gardens, schools, volunteer cleanup days, landscaping crews or a large household that likes gloves everywhere. It means a clean pair is always available and nobody fights over a muddy one. A wrinkled surface is a texture that channels moisture, which is why it is used in many disposable work gloves.

The pack size means quality control is looser, and the gloves are a basic, lighter-duty build than the others here. You would not choose this for a single gardener, since the gloves can degrade in storage and take up space. Compared with the Wells Lamont, the WHEATHUSK is far more pairs and less refined. Store the box in a cool, dry place away from sun.
products.bestFor: Groups, volunteer events and crews that need many pairs of simple grippy gloves.
pros: One hundred pairs for large groups
Wrinkled nitrile grips wet and dry
cons: Too many pairs for one gardener

buyingCriteria.explanation: Gauge counts the stitches per inch in the liner, and a higher number means a thinner, more sensitive glove. The Wells Lamont and NEOTRIL list a 13 gauge shell, which is fine and flexible, while the PROMEDIX and Atlas describe lightweight knits without a gauge. Pick a fine gauge for planting and sorting, and a thicker liner for pulling weeds in cool weather. A fine gauge feels wonderful in June and chilly in March.

Foam nitrile has tiny pockets that let a glove grip and breathe a little, while smooth nitrile gives a tougher but slicker surface. The PROMEDIX uses foamed nitrile, the LOCCEF and NEOTRIL use micro-foam, and the WHEATHUSK uses a wrinkled coating. For wet gardening, foam or wrinkle texture is the better choice. For oily or abrasive work, a thicker smooth coating wears longer.

Nitrile gloves wear out at the thumb and forefinger, so more pairs is a practical advantage. The WHEATHUSK offers one hundred pairs, the LOCCEF six, the Wells Lamont five and the Atlas and PROMEDIX four each. Buy a larger pack if several people share the gloves or if you use them for painting and household work as well. Thumbs go first, so check that corner when you decide a pair is finished.

Stitching on the finger can rub a blister during hours of repetitive work. The LOCCEF and NEOTRIL list seamless liners, which removes that problem. Check the listing for the word seamless, and try the glove on before a long day of transplanting. A small amount of rubbing becomes a real irritation after an hour.

A knit wrist holds the glove on and keeps soil out, but a longer cuff covers more of the wrist. The PROMEDIX has extended flexible cuffs, the Wells Lamont and LOCCEF have knit wrists, and the Atlas is elastic. Short cuffs are easier to pull on, and longer ones help when you reach into beds. Pick the cuff that matches how often you reach under shrubs.

Nitrile can crack after long UV exposure, so store gloves away from direct sun. The NEOTRIL lists machine washing and quick drying, while others suggest hand washing and air drying. Avoid hot water and fabric softener, both of which can damage coatings. Hang gloves to dry with fingers pointing down.

howWeEvaluated.title: Dexterity
howWeEvaluated.description: We ranked gloves by shell thickness and seam construction. The Wells Lamont and NEOTRIL with their 13 gauge shells and the Atlas with its ultra-light liner lead, the seamless LOCCEF follows, and the PROMEDIX and WHEATHUSK come next. Dexterity matters most for planting and potting.

howWeEvaluated.title: Grip
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared coating textures. The LOCCEF and NEOTRIL micro-foam and the PROMEDIX foamed nitrile lead, the WHEATHUSK wrinkled surface follows, and the Atlas and Wells Lamont use plain palm coatings. Wet grip is the main reason to choose nitrile.

howWeEvaluated.title: Durability
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at reinforcement and coating thickness. The PROMEDIX thickened fingertips and Wells Lamont abrasion resistance lead, the LOCCEF follows, and the thinner bulk and light duty packs come last. None of these is credited for thorn protection.

howWeEvaluated.title: Pack value
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted pairs per pack. The WHEATHUSK leads by far, the LOCCEF and Wells Lamont follow with six and five pairs, and the Atlas, PROMEDIX and NEOTRIL offer smaller packs. More pairs reduce the cost of wear.

howWeEvaluated.title: Care
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked maintenance notes. The NEOTRIL lists machine washing, the LOCCEF and Wells Lamont suggest standard washing, and the others rely on hand washing. Easy care keeps gloves usable longer.

cards.label: Foam and micro-foam
cards.text: The PROMEDIX, LOCCEF and NEOTRIL use foamed or micro-foam nitrile. The air pockets give grip and some breathability, and they grip well on wet stems. They are slightly less tough than a thick smooth coating.

cards.label: Smooth or wrinkled
cards.text: The Atlas, Wells Lamont and WHEATHUSK use plain or wrinkled nitrile. They resist abrasion and wipe clean easily. They can be slicker on wet surfaces unless the texture is deep.

howToChoose.note: Foam is the better choice for damp gardening, and smooth for dry abrasive jobs.

faq.q: Is nitrile better than latex for gardening gloves?
faq.a: Nitrile resists oils and punctures a little better and does not trigger latex allergies. Latex is more elastic and often softer. For most gardeners the choice comes down to allergy concerns and the texture of the coating.
No. A thin coating over a knit will not stop a hooked rose thorn, and sources disagree on how much puncture resistance it adds. Use a leather glove with a long cuff for roses and brambles.

It refers to the number of stitches per inch in the knit liner. A higher number means a finer, thinner glove with better feel. The Wells Lamont and NEOTRIL list 13 gauge shells, which are suited to light and precise work.

faq.q: How do I clean nitrile coated gloves?
faq.a: Rinse off soil and wash with mild soap, following the maker's directions. The NEOTRIL lists machine washing, and others are safest by hand. Air dry them away from heat and direct sun.

faq.q: Why do my nitrile gloves crack?
faq.a: Long UV exposure and heat make the coating brittle. Store gloves in a cool, shaded place, and avoid leaving them in a hot car. Replace any glove with cracks at the palm.

faq.q: How many pairs should I buy?
faq.a: Two to four pairs cover most households, so you can rotate while one dries. A larger pack such as the LOCCEF or Wells Lamont suits shared use. The WHEATHUSK is meant for groups.

faq.q: Can I use nitrile gloves for chemical sprays?
faq.a: These are gardening gloves, not chemical-resistant gloves. Always read the label of any spray or fertilizer and use the protective gear it specifies. Do not assume a coated knit glove is rated for chemicals.
